sentences.text: A narrow, grassy footpath wound through the fields, as unhurried as the stream it followed.
The steep, flinty track climbed relentlessly uphill, and soon every breath was an effort.
Thick, glutinous mud sucked at his boots, reluctant to give back each step.
The sodden, waterlogged field squelched underfoot, and cold water welled up around their ankles.
At a weathered, wooden stile the path forked in two, and neither branch looked more trodden than the other.
The faint, forgotten trail dwindled into the long grass and was gone, as if it had lost heart.
Loose, pale gravel crunched beneath their boots, announcing them long before they reached the door.
The dry, dusty lane twisted between the hedgerows, each bend hiding the next.
The slick, moss-covered steps descended into shadow, and nobody offered to go first.
On the dark, overgrown bridleway he stumbled over a root, and brambles closed behind him like a door.
The rain had left deep, brimming puddles along the lane, and the children splashed through every one.
The path dipped into a hollow and then skirted the edge of the wood, keeping the trees at arm's length.
They trudged along the track, heads bowed against the driving rain, stepping over deep, water-filled ruts.
The old road crumbled at the edges, where weeds had prised the tarmac apart.
They ambled arm in arm down the quiet, dappled lane, in no hurry to arrive anywhere.
High above the gorge, the path narrowed to a muddy ledge no wider than a boot.
She skipped down the path, swinging her bag, scattering sparrows from the verge.
The cart rattled into the square, its wheels jolting over the smooth, worn cobbles.
They scrambled up the embankment and collapsed onto soft, springy turf.
The long, deserted road stretched ahead of them, ruled straight across the plain without a house or a tree.
A path led down to the river through a thick carpet of copper leaves.
Rough, uneven ground slowed them to a crawl, and twice she turned her ankle.
Frost had turned the mud to iron-hard, frozen earth that rang beneath their boots.
Fresh, muddy footprints crossed the yard and stopped, inexplicably, at a blank wall.
After weeks without rain, the path was nothing but parched, cracked earth, pale as bone.
In the early light, dew turned the verge to a strip of scattered diamonds.
The storm turned the track into a torrent of mud that swept stones and branches down the hill.
Moss had softened the old path until footsteps made no sound at all.
The sunken, shadowy lane ran between banks so high that it felt like walking along the bottom of a trench.
Grass grew down the middle of the track; no cart had passed that way in years.
